title: Dietary reference values for vitamin K
authors: EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies (NDA), Turck D, Bresson JL, Burlingame B, Dean T, Fairweather-Tait S, et al.
funder: European Food Safety Authority, on request from the European Commission (question EFSA-Q-2011-01232).
result: Vitamin K is the cofactor of gamma-glutamyl carboxylase (GGCX), which converts glutamic acid residues of vitamin K-dependent proteins, including coagulation factors II, VII, IX and X and the anticoagulant proteins C, S and Z, into calcium-binding gamma-carboxyglutamic acid residues; vitamin K hydroquinone is converted to vitamin K epoxide and reduced back by vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR), the step of the cycle blocked by warfarin. In adults, deficiency causes a bleeding tendency with a vitamin K-responsive increase in prothrombin time. In infants not given vitamin K prophylaxis, late vitamin K deficiency bleeding occurred in 4.4 to 7.2 per 100,000 births in Western European countries; its relative risk without prophylaxis is estimated at 81.
